query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by their high configurational entropy, which stabilizes a single-phase solid solution and minimizes phase segregation and atomic diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneously synthesized near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with a single solid-solution phase and uniform lattice structure.
generation.intervention: Post-synthesis heat treatment in a reactive atmosphere designed to selectively reduce or deplete one of the constituent elements, thereby intentionally lowering the configurational entropy.
generation.conditions: Service conditions simulating catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric use (473–1923 K) in inert or controlled atmospheres to minimize oxidative effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy that enforces a disordered but stable atomic distribution and uniform coordination environment across the nanoparticle.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy reduces the driving force for phase segregation and intermetallic precipitation under thermal stress by lowering the free energy difference between the single-solid solution and segregated phases. This slows atomic diffusion and maintains uniform active sites necessary for catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that retain high configurational entropy (i.e., the pristine HEA nanoparticles) will exhibit minimal phase separation, lower atomic diffusion, and stable structural as well as catalytic/thermoelectric performances relative to nanoparticles subjected to entropy-reducing post-synthesis treatments.
generation.baseline: Pristine HEA nanoparticles synthesized via established methods with near-equiatomic homogeneity, not subjected to any entropy-reducing interventions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature regimes (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) and is contingent on the maintenance of inert or controlled atmospheres during operation to prevent extrinsic oxidation effects.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative threshold of configurational entropy required for stability and the sensitivity of stability to small compositional deviations remain uncertain, warranting further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: (A) pristine near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with high configurational entropy, and (B) nanoparticles subjected to post-synthesis heat treatment in a reactive atmosphere to selectively deplete one element, thereby lowering the configurational entropy. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature conditions matching catalytic (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operation in an inert atmosphere. Examine the structural stability via X-ray diffraction and TEM, and assess catalytic performance using standard electrochemical reactions (e.g., HER, ORR, OER).
measurements: Phase integrity and lattice structure using X-ray diffraction
Morphology and elemental distribution using TEM and EDS mapping
Catalytic performance through electrochemical testing (LSV, current density, overpotential)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the entropy-reduced nanoparticles (set B) exhibit structural and catalytic/thermoelectric stabilities that are statistically indistinguishable from those of the pristine nanoparticles (set A) under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy governs the stability of these nanoparticles will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. Since the successful fabrication of the first-ever entropy- stabilized oxides, or, more general, high-entropy oxides (HEOs), such solid solutions have drawn much attention due to their unique compositional and structural features, namely, the extreme chemical disorder incorporated into single-crystal structures (). One representative example is that the metal ions in (Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)O are unanimously divalent and randomly occupy the cationic sites in a rocksalt structure. These cations are coordinated by lattice oxygen in an octahedral configuration, even though Cu(II) and Zn(II) are usually four coordinated to oxygen atoms as, for example, in their binary oxides (). This stabilization of Cu(II) and Zn(II) in an unfavorable configuration is ascribable to the increased configurational entropy and a high solid solution temperature (, , ). Inspired by rocksalt HEOs, researchers have undertaken extensive work to develop diverse types of HEOs. HEOs in different crystal structures have been synthesized accordingly in the past decade, such as fluorite (, ), perovskite (), spinel (), bixbyite (), and pyrochlore (, ). cited_evidence.text: The exploration of HEA nanoparticles as electrocatalysts represents a burgeoning field of research with the potential to revolutionize energy conversion and storage technologies []. Figure 10a presents the LSV plots illustrating the multi-functional catalyst applications of the HEA nanoparticles. These curves reveal the particles’ ability to catalyze key reactions: HER, ORR, and OER. This multi-faceted catalytic capability opens new avenues for technological advancements. The multi-functional nature of these HEA nanoparticles as catalysts offers promising opportunities for their use in diverse energy technologies, including fuel cells, electrolyzers, and metal–air batteries. Their distinctive properties have the potential to enhance the efficiency, sustainability, and cost-effectiveness of energy conversion and storage systems.
